title: Rhyming words
keyIdea: Two words rhyme when they end with the same sound: cat and hat both end in at. The start can be different. Words that start the same, like cat and cup, do not rhyme, and words that sound close, like bed and bell, do not rhyme either. Rhyme is about sound, not spelling: bear and chair rhyme. In poems and songs, rhymes often come at the ends of lines.
familyTip: Play a rhyme game on a walk. Say a word, like tree, and take turns to say words that rhyme: bee, see, key. Silly made-up words count too. When you read a rhyming book together, stop before the last word of a line and let your child say it.

visual.caption: Does it rhyme with bee? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: fill the cat train with rhymes, find the odd one out, reject close misses, find rhymes in a poem, match long rhymes.

kid: Cat and hat rhyme. Say them out loud: c-at, h-at. They end with the same sound, at. Words that rhyme have the same end sound. The start can be different.
A word can start like cat and still not rhyme. Cat and cup both start with c, but cup ends in up. Bed and bell sound close, but bell ends in ll. To rhyme, the whole end has to match.
Rhyme is about sound, not letters. Bear and chair do not look the same. But say them: they both end in air, so they rhyme. Say the words and listen. Do not just look.

Poems and songs have lots of rhymes. Often the rhyme comes at the end of a line: A big brown bear sat on a chair. Long words can rhyme too, when the last part sounds the same: honey and money, kitten and mitten.
adult: Ages 4 to 6. This matches CCSS RF.K.2.a, recognize and produce rhyming words. It also matches the National Curriculum in England for Year 1 reading: recognising and joining in with predictable phrases, and learning to appreciate rhymes and poems. In the EYFS, Development Matters asks 3 and 4 year olds to spot and suggest rhymes. Key words: rhyme, rhyming words, end sound, onset, rime, phonological awareness, alliteration, line, poem.

Two words rhyme when they share the rime: the last stressed vowel sound and everything after it. Cat and hat share at. Honey and money share the part from the stressed vowel on, oney. Rhyme is a sound skill, so it is judged by ear. Spelling can differ (bear, chair, where), and words that look alike may not rhyme (cow, low). Hearing rhyme is one of the early steps in phonological awareness, before splitting words into single sounds for phonics.

Common mistakes: hearing words that start the same (cat, cup) as a rhyme, which is alliteration; accepting near misses that share the start and the middle sound (bed, bell); judging by letters, not sound; picking a word with a linked meaning (cat, kitten); and, in longer words, matching the start (honey, hammer) not the end. The lab, the practice and the challenge target each of these.

In the lab your child lets only rhymes for cat onto a train, and car and cup are turned away. They find the odd one out in four sets. They pick the words that rhyme with bed but not bell or web. They find the rhyming words at the ends of the lines of a short poem, and match honey, kitten and flower to their rhymes. Each word is spoken when they tap it, if the device can speak.

practice.hint: Say each word with cat. Which one ends with at?
practice.explain: Hat and cat both end in at, so they rhyme. Cup starts like cat, but its end is different.

practice.prompt: You find {n} pairs of rhyming words, like cat and hat. Each pair has 2 words. How many words is that?
practice.hint: Each pair is 2 words. Count 2 for every pair.
practice.explain: {n} pairs with 2 words in each is {=2*n} words.

choices: No, only the start is the same
Yes, they both start with s
practice.hint: Rhyming words end the same. Listen to the ends: s-un, s-ock.
practice.explain: Sun ends in un and sock ends in ock. Only the start is the same, so they do not rhyme.

practice.prompt: {n} bees sit in a tree. Which word rhymes with bee?
practice.hint: Say bee, then each word. Which one ends with ee?
practice.explain: Bee and tree both end in ee, so they rhyme. Bus and bell only start like bee.

practice.prompt: Which word sounds close to bed but does not rhyme with it?
practice.hint: Find the word that has the same start but a different end.
practice.explain: Bell starts like bed, but it ends in ll, not ed. Red and sled do rhyme with bed.

pool.hint: Say fox, then each word. Listen for the end, ox.
pool.explain: Fox and box both end in ox. Fish and frog start like fox, but that is not a rhyme.

pool.prompt: Cake, snake, kite. Which one does not rhyme?
pool.hint: Two of them end with ake. Which one does not?
pool.explain: Cake and snake end in ake. Kite ends in ite, so it is the odd one out.

pool.prompt: Bear and chair are spelt in different ways. Do they rhyme?
choices: Yes, they end with the same sound
pool.hint: Say them out loud. Rhyme is about sound.
pool.explain: Bear and chair both end with the sound air. They rhyme, even though the letters are different.

pool.hint: In a long word, listen to the last part: hon-ey.
pool.explain: Honey and money both end in oney. Hammer and hungry start like honey, but their ends are different.

pool.prompt: You say {n} words that rhyme with cat. Then you think of 1 more. How many rhyming words do you have now?
pool.hint: Count on 1 from the words you already have.
pool.explain: {n} and 1 more is {=n+1} words that rhyme with cat.

choices: They end with the same sound
They start with the same sound
pool.hint: Think of cat and hat. What part is the same?
pool.explain: Rhyming words have the same end sound, like cat and hat. The start can be different.

pool.prompt: {n} goats want to sail away. Which word rhymes with goat?
pool.hint: Say goat, then each word. Listen for the end, oat.
pool.explain: Goat and boat both end in oat, so the {n} goats need a boat. Goal sounds close and gate starts the same, but their ends are different.

pool.hint: Find the two words that end the same way.
pool.explain: Kitten and mitten both end in itten. Cat means a grown-up kitten but does not rhyme, and kettle only starts the same.

pool.prompt: In a poem, where do the rhymes often go?
choices: At the ends of the lines
At the start of each line
pool.hint: A big brown bear sat on a chair. Where are bear and chair?
pool.explain: Rhymes often go at the ends of lines, like bear and chair. That helps you guess the next rhyme.
